UAV Research Onboarding

Linux, Git, ROS 2, PX4 and Gazebo, for newcomers

Abstract

This guide teaches the minimum you need to start work in a UAV research group. It assumes you have never used Linux, Git, ROS 2, PX4 or Gazebo. It covers only the tools a typical group uses: Ubuntu, ROS 2, PX4 firmware with Gazebo simulation, and a ground station. Isaac Sim will be added in a later version. Read it once, then use the First-day checklist on your first day.

1 Versions

Everything below targets these versions. When the group upgrades, change this table and check the commands that mention a version.

Component Version Note
Ubuntu 24.04 lsb_release -a
ROS 2 Jazzy docs: docs.ros.org/en/jazzy
PX4 firmware 1.17 docs: use the page for 1.17
px4_msgs branch release/1.17 must match the firmware
Gazebo Harmonic (gz) as installed by the PX4 setup script
Micro XRCE-DDS Agent as installed in the lab MicroXRCEAgent
QGroundControl current stable ground station

2 Linux

2.1 The terminal and the filesystem

Almost all work happens in a terminal. You type a command, press Enter, and read the output. The shell (here bash or zsh) is the program that reads your commands.

Linux has one directory tree that starts at / (the root). Your own files live in your home directory, written ~ (for example /home/riccardo). A path says where a file is. An absolute path starts with / or ~. A relative path starts from the current directory. The path . is the current directory and .. is its parent.

pwd                       # print the current directory
ls -l                     # list files, one per line, with details
cd ~/my_repo              # change directory
cd ..                     # go to the parent directory
mkdir -p ws/src           # make a directory (and parents)
cp a.txt b.txt            # copy;   mv a.txt c.txt  moves or renames
rm b.txt                  # delete a file (no recycle bin!)
cat file.txt              # print a file;  less file.txt  to scroll
grep -rn "offboard" src/  # search text in files
man ls                    # manual page of a command (q to quit)

Tips: press Tab to complete names. Press the up arrow to recall old commands. Press Ctrl-R to search your history. File names are case sensitive.

2.2 Permissions and sudo

Each file has an owner and three permission sets: owner, group, others. Each set allows read (r), write (w) and execute (x). ls -l shows them, for example -rwxr-xr-x. A script must have the execute bit to run as ./script.sh.

chmod +x script.sh        # make a file executable
sudo apt update           # run one command as administrator

Use sudo only when a command needs it (installing system packages). Never run ROS or your own code with sudo.

2.3 Environment variables and source

An environment variable is a named string that programs can read. ROS 2 depends on them. Print one with echo $ROS_DISTRO. Set one for the current shell with export ROS_DOMAIN_ID=7.

A setup file such as /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash sets many variables at once (it extends PATH, the list of folders where the shell looks for programs). You must source it, not run it:

source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash

Sourcing changes only the current terminal. When you open a new terminal you must source again, or put the line in ~/.bashrc (read at the start of every bash terminal). A frequent beginner error is “command not found” for ros2 or colcon: you forgot to source.

Note

If your shell is zsh, source the .zsh file instead (/opt/ros/jazzy/setup.zsh) and put the line in ~/.zshrc.

Tip

Put the base ROS 2 setup file (setup.bash or setup.zsh) in your shell startup file. Source the overlay of your workspace (install/setup.bash) only when you work in that workspace (Workspaces and colcon).

2.4 Installing software with apt

Ubuntu installs system software with apt.

sudo apt update                        # refresh the package list
sudo apt install git build-essential   # install packages
apt search ros-jazzy-rqt               # search

2.5 Processes

Every running program is a process. Press Ctrl-C in a terminal to stop the program in it. Ctrl-Z suspends it. If a program hangs, or a simulator stays alive in the background:

ps aux | grep -i gz        # find processes whose line contains "gz"
kill 12345                 # ask process 12345 to stop (12345 is the PID)
kill -9 12345              # force it, if the first kill did not work
pkill -f px4               # kill by name pattern
htop                       # live process viewer (q to quit)

You will run several programs at once (the simulator, the bridge to PX4, your own nodes). Use one terminal for each, or a terminal multiplexer such as tmux.

2.6 SSH into the onboard computer

The drone carries a small computer. You log in to it over the network with SSH.

Note

The lab drones are already set up. Read this section for background, and use it when you set up new hardware.

ssh-keygen -t ed25519              # once: make a key pair
ssh-copy-id user@drone-ip          # copy the public key to the drone
ssh user@drone-ip                  # log in; type "exit" to leave
scp file.txt user@drone-ip:~/      # copy a file to the drone

Ask your supervisor for the user name and the IP address of the onboard computer; they are not written here on purpose. The same key type is used to push to GitHub (Git and GitHub).

2.7 Editors

Use what you like. Recommended editors:

  • VS Code: the most used in the group. Its “Remote - SSH” extension edits files on the drone.

  • Zed: built in Rust, faster.

  • Neovim: not beginner friendly.

nano file is the simplest terminal editor (Ctrl-O saves, Ctrl-X exits). If you land in vim by accident, press Esc, then type :q! and Enter to leave.

3 Git and GitHub

Git records the history of a folder (a repository). Each saved state is a commit. GitHub hosts a copy of the repository online and adds issues and pull requests. Lab repositories are usually private. Ask for access, add your SSH public key (~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub) in your GitHub account settings, and test with ssh -T git@github.com.

3.1 Daily commands

git clone --recursive git@github.com:<owner>/<repo>.git
cd <repo>
git status                  # what changed?
git diff                    # show the changes in detail
git add src/my_node.cpp     # stage a file for the next commit
git commit -m "feat(controller): add acceleration limit"
git push                    # upload your commits
git pull                    # download and merge new commits
git log --oneline -10       # last 10 commits

The flow is: edit files, git add the ones that belong together, git commit with a message, git push. A commit is local until you push.

Write commit messages as Conventional Commits: <type>(<scope>): <description>, for example feat(controller): add acceleration limit or fix(bridge): correct frame conversion.

3.2 Branches

A branch is a movable label for a line of commits. Do your work on a branch, not on main.

git switch -c feat/12-hover-node       # make and switch to a new branch
git switch main                        # go back
git push -u origin feat/12-hover-node  # first push of a new branch

Branch names start with the type (feat, fix, docs, chore) and should contain the issue number.

3.3 Commit messages

Messages follow Conventional Commits: type(scope): description. Examples:

feat(controller): add tilt limit
fix(mapper): clamp negative distance
docs(guide): add ROS 2 section

Use the imperative, lower case, no final period. Add refs #12 (or fixes #12) at the end of the body to link the commit to an issue.

3.4 Issues and pull requests

An issue describes one task. Check the open issues before you start, and write one for new work. A pull request (PR) asks to merge your branch into main. Someone reviews it, then it is merged. If git pull reports a conflict, Git marks the clashing lines with <<<<<<<; edit the file to keep what you want, git add it, and git commit.

3.5 Submodules

A project can include another repository inside it. A typical case in a PX4 project is the message package:

Path Content Pinned to
src/px4_msgs PX4 message definitions (public) branch release/1.17 (e.g. tag v1.17.0)

A submodule is pinned to one commit. The parent repo does not store the files of the submodule. It stores the URL (in .gitmodules) and one exact commit hash. When you clone, you get that commit and nothing else, so everyone builds the same code.

# add it once, following the firmware's release branch
git submodule add -b release/1.17 \
  https://github.com/PX4/px4_msgs.git src/px4_msgs

# fresh clone with everything, including nested submodules
git clone --recursive git@github.com:<owner>/<repo>.git

# you cloned without --recursive, or someone bumped a submodule:
git submodule update --init --recursive

git submodule status        # shows the pinned hash of each one

A leading + in the status means the submodule folder is at a different commit than the parent pins. A leading - means it is not initialised yet. After a plain git pull in the parent, run git submodule update --init --recursive so the folders follow the new pins.

Bumping a submodule. To move px4_msgs to a newer commit of its release branch:

cd src/px4_msgs
git fetch && git switch release/1.17 && git pull   # get the new commit
cd ../..
git status        # shows: modified: src/px4_msgs (new commits)
git add src/px4_msgs
git commit -m "build: bump px4_msgs"

Rule: if you change code inside a submodule you own, commit and push it there first, then commit the new pin in the parent. If you do it in the other order, other people cannot fetch the pinned commit. Do not bump px4_msgs on your own to a different release line: it must match the PX4 firmware (PX4).

4 ROS 2

ROS 2 is a set of libraries and tools to build robot software as many small programs that talk to each other. This guide uses Ubuntu 24.04 and ROS 2 Jazzy (see Versions). Use Jazzy commands and documentation (docs.ros.org/en/jazzy); older tutorials may differ.

4.1 Installing ROS 2 Jazzy

A new machine has no ROS 2. Check with ls /opt/ros: if the folder is missing or does not list jazzy, install the deb packages, following the official Ubuntu install page. Do the steps in order and check the output of each before the next.

  1. Check that the locale supports UTF-8 (for example en_US.UTF-8). If it does not, the install page shows how to set one.

    locale

  2. Enable the Ubuntu universe repository.

    sudo apt install software-properties-common
sudo add-apt-repository universe

  3. Add the ROS 2 apt repository. One package installs its keys and sources. Run these four lines in the same terminal: the second line sets a variable that the third line uses.

    sudo apt update && sudo apt install curl -y
export ROS_APT_SOURCE_VERSION=$(curl -s https://api.github.com/repos/ros-infrastructure/ros-apt-source/releases/latest | grep -F "tag_name" | awk -F'"' '{print $4}')
curl -L -o /tmp/ros2-apt-source.deb "https://github.com/ros-infrastructure/ros-apt-source/releases/download/${ROS_APT_SOURCE_VERSION}/ros2-apt-source_${ROS_APT_SOURCE_VERSION}.$(. /etc/os-release && echo ${UBUNTU_CODENAME:-${VERSION_CODENAME}})_all.deb"
sudo dpkg -i /tmp/ros2-apt-source.deb

  4. Update the system. ROS 2 packages are built against an up-to-date Ubuntu.

    sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade

  5. Install ROS 2 and the build tools. ros-jazzy-desktop includes RViz, the demos and the tutorials; ros-dev-tools brings colcon. If ros-dev-tools fails with dependency conflicts, the install page has the fix.

    sudo apt install ros-jazzy-desktop ros-dev-tools

  6. Test the install. In one terminal start a talker:

    source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash
ros2 run demo_nodes_cpp talker

    In a second terminal start a listener:

    source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash
ros2 run demo_nodes_py listener

    The talker prints Publishing lines and the listener prints I heard lines.

4.2 Installing the other tools

A new machine also needs these. Follow the official page for each:

  • PX4-Autopilot and Gazebo: PX4 Ubuntu development environment. Its ubuntu.sh script installs the PX4 toolchain and Gazebo.

  • Micro XRCE-DDS Agent: PX4 ROS 2 user guide, “Setup the Agent”. It builds the agent inside your ROS 2 workspace.

  • QGroundControl: QGC download and install.

4.3 Concepts

  • A node is one program with one job (for example a mapper, or a controller).

  • A topic is a named channel, such as /camera/depth/points. A node publishes messages to it; other nodes subscribe and receive them.

  • A message is a typed record. Its type, like px4_msgs/msg/TrajectorySetpoint, lists named fields (position, velocity, acceleration, …).

  • A parameter is a named setting of a node (a gain, a horizon length) that you set at start or change at run time.

  • A launch file (Python) starts many nodes with their parameters in one command.

Nodes do not know each other. They only know topic names and types. So a simulated sensor and a real sensor can be exchanged without changing the controller.

4.4 QoS: why PX4 topics need special settings

Quality of Service (QoS) settings decide how messages are delivered. A publisher and a subscriber only connect if their settings are compatible. The two settings that matter here:

  • Reliability: reliable resends lost messages; best effort does not. Sensor streams use best effort, since a late old sample is worse than a lost one.

  • Durability: volatile sends only to subscribers present at publish time; transient local keeps the last message for late subscribers.

The ROS 2 default for a subscriber is reliable and volatile. PX4 does not use these defaults, so a default subscriber to a PX4 topic can silently receive nothing, which is the most common beginner failure. The PX4 documentation says subscribers “must specify a appropriate (compatible) QoS setting” and uses the predefined sensor-data profile (rmw_qos_profile_sensor_data: best effort, volatile, small queue) for PX4 output topics; its example sets a depth of 5. The guide gives no per-topic settings, so use that profile for every PX4 topic. Publishers to /fmu/in/ need no special QoS: the ROS 2 default is compatible. If a subscription shows no data, check with ros2 topic info -v <topic>, which prints the QoS of each endpoint.

4.5 Workspaces and colcon

Your code lives in a workspace: a folder with a src/ directory. colcon builds every package in src/.

source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash
cd ~/my_repo
colcon build --packages-select px4_msgs     # build one package
source install/setup.bash                   # make the result visible

Colcon creates build/, install/ and log/. Never edit them and never commit them. The order matters: first source the ROS base install (the underlay), then build, then source install/setup.bash (the overlay) in every new terminal where you want to run your packages. Build only what you changed with --packages-select; large packages can be slow to compile.

4.6 Command line tools

ros2 topic list                              # all topics
ros2 topic info /fmu/out/vehicle_status -v   # type and QoS (name may differ)
ros2 topic echo <topic>                      # print messages
ros2 topic hz <topic>                        # publication rate
ros2 interface show px4_msgs/msg/TrajectorySetpoint   # message fields
ros2 node list                               # running nodes
ros2 param list /my_node                     # parameters of a node
ros2 launch <package> <file>.launch.py       # start a launch file
rqt_graph                                    # picture of nodes and topics
rviz2                                        # 3D view: clouds, maps, paths

Before you use a message field, check its name with ros2 interface show. If two people on one network see each other’s topics by accident, set a different ROS_DOMAIN_ID (0 to 101) in each terminal.

4.7 A minimal node

A subscriber in Python (rclpy) that prints the north position from PX4, with a compatible QoS. The field x exists in px4_msgs/msg/VehicleLocalPosition; it is the north position in the NED frame, in metres (checked in the msg folder of px4_msgs). The topic name must be checked with ros2 topic list (PX4).

import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from rclpy.qos import qos_profile_sensor_data
from px4_msgs.msg import VehicleLocalPosition

class Echo(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__("echo")
        self.create_subscription(
            VehicleLocalPosition, "/fmu/out/vehicle_local_position",
            self.cb, qos_profile_sensor_data)

    def cb(self, msg):
        self.get_logger().info(f"north = {msg.x:.2f} m")

rclpy.init()
rclpy.spin(Echo())

Run it with python3 echo.py in a terminal where both ROS and the workspace are sourced. C++ nodes (rclcpp) have the same structure: create the node, create subscriptions and publishers, spin.

5 PX4

5.1 Architecture

PX4 is the flight-controller firmware. It runs on the flight-controller board (or, in simulation, as a normal program on your PC). It reads the IMU and other sensors, estimates the vehicle state (with an EKF), and runs the control loops that turn setpoints into motor commands. Inside PX4, modules communicate through uORB, a publish/subscribe system like ROS topics but internal to the firmware. PX4 does not run ROS. A bridge (uXRCE-DDS bridge) copies chosen uORB topics to ROS 2.

Control is hierarchical. Your controller outputs a setpoint, for example an acceleration. PX4’s position and velocity controllers turn it into an attitude and thrust setpoint; the attitude and rate loops close the rest at a much higher rate. This is why a high-level planner can often treat the vehicle as a point mass: the fast inner loops are PX4’s job.

5.2 Flight modes and offboard mode

A flight mode decides who produces the setpoints. Manual and stabilised modes follow the pilot’s sticks. Position mode holds position. Hold, Return and Land are automatic. Offboard mode follows setpoints that arrive from an external computer, which is your ROS 2 node.

Rules for offboard mode, from the PX4 documentation:

  • PX4 must already receive OffboardControlMode messages before it accepts offboard mode or arms in it. Start the stream first.

  • OffboardControlMode must be sent together with a setpoint message (for example TrajectorySetpoint). The first message says which fields are used; the second carries the values.

  • If the stream of OffboardControlMode drops below about 2 Hz, PX4 leaves offboard mode (failsafe). Send both at a steady rate well above that. The official example uses a 100 ms timer (10 Hz); 50 Hz or more is common.

  • The official example sends 10 setpoints, then requests the mode switch, then arms.

The three messages (fields checked in the msg folder of px4_msgs):

  • OffboardControlMode: timestamp and the booleans position, velocity, acceleration, attitude, body_rate, thrust_and_torque, direct_actuator. For acceleration control set acceleration = true and the others false.

  • TrajectorySetpoint: timestamp, position[3], velocity[3], acceleration[3], jerk[3], yaw, yawspeed. In NED, metres and seconds. Set every field you do not control to NaN: the message file says NaN means “the state should not be controlled”. For example, to command an acceleration, set acceleration and leave position and velocity NaN.

  • VehicleCommand: command, param1, param2, …, target_system, target_component, source_system, source_component, from_external. Arm with the command VEHICLE_CMD_COMPONENT_ARM_DISARM (400), param1 = 1. Switch mode with VEHICLE_CMD_DO_SET_MODE (176); the official example uses param1 = 1 and param2 = 6 for offboard.

To see the current mode, read VehicleStatus: its nav_state equals NAVIGATION_STATE_OFFBOARD (14) and arming_state equals ARMING_STATE_ARMED (2) when all is well.

5.3 The uXRCE-DDS bridge

PX4 talks to ROS 2 through the Micro XRCE-DDS protocol. A client runs inside PX4 and an agent runs on the companion computer (or the PC in simulation). The agent exposes the PX4 topics as ROS 2 topics under the prefix /fmu/: PX4 output under /fmu/out/, input under /fmu/in/. Start it for the simulator:

MicroXRCEAgent udp4 -p 8888

The PX4 ROS 2 guide uses this command. On the real drone the link is a serial line. On our drone the agent runs as MicroXRCEAgent serial --dev /dev/ttyTHS1 -b 921600, and PX4 has UXRCE_DDS_CFG = TELEM2 at 921600 baud. Expect names such as /fmu/in/offboard_control_mode, /fmu/in/trajectory_setpoint, /fmu/in/vehicle_command. Since PX4 1.16 some messages are versioned (the MESSAGE_VERSION constant in the .msg files), which may add a suffix to the topic name. Always run ros2 topic list and use what you see.

px4_msgs must match the firmware. The bridge sends messages as raw binary. If the field layout in your ROS 2 package differs from the one compiled into the firmware, data is misread or dropped. Pin src/px4_msgs to the release branch of your firmware (release/1.17 for PX4 1.17, see Submodules). If the firmware changes, change the submodule with it, and rebuild with colcon build --packages-select px4_msgs.

5.4 Frames: NED/FRD versus ENU/FLU

PX4 and ROS use different frame conventions, and mixing them up is the most common source of bugs.

ROS (REP-103) PX4
World frame ENU: x East, y North, z Up NED: x North, y East, z Down
Body frame FLU: x forward, y left, z up FRD: x forward, y right, z down

Consequences:

  • Altitude is −z in PX4. Flying 2 m above the ground means z = −2 in the position of TrajectorySetpoint and in VehicleLocalPosition.z. A positive z setpoint drives the drone into the floor.

  • World vectors convert ENU to NED by swapping x and y and negating z: (xE, yN, zU) ↦ (yN, xE, −zU). The PX4 docs describe it as a rotation of π/2 about Z then π about X.

  • Body vectors convert FLU to FRD (and back) by negating y and z (a rotation of π about X).

  • Yaw: PX4 yaw is measured from North, positive clockwise seen from above; ROS yaw is measured from East, positive counter-clockwise. A conversion is needed here too.

The PX4 docs recommend the helper functions in px4_ros_com (frame_transforms). Decide once, in your project, in which frame each node works and convert only at the PX4 boundary. Many ROS nodes use ENU internally; the setpoint is then converted to NED just before publishing. An acceleration setpoint is a world-frame acceleration, so the same x ↔︎ y, z → −z rule applies to it.

5.5 Simulation: SITL with Gazebo

SITL (software in the loop) runs the real PX4 firmware as a program on your PC, with Gazebo (gz) simulating the drone and the world. You need your own PX4-Autopilot checkout in ~/PX4-Autopilot, at tag v1.17.0 (not part of your project repo; see Installing the other tools). The make targets from the PX4 docs are:

cd ~/PX4-Autopilot        # path is machine-specific
make px4_sitl gz_x500                 # plain x500 quadrotor
make px4_sitl gz_x500_depth           # x500 with a front depth camera
make px4_sitl gz_x500_lidar_2d        # x500 with a 2D LiDAR

These three targets are listed in the PX4 Gazebo page (main documentation). A world is chosen by appending its name to the target or with the environment variable PX4_GZ_WORLD. The first build takes several minutes. Simulated sensor images and point clouds reach ROS 2 through a Gazebo-ROS bridge (package ros_gz_bridge); the topic names depend on the model.

5.6 QGroundControl, parameters and safety

QGroundControl (QGC) is the ground-station program. It shows the vehicle state, lets you arm, change the flight mode, read and write PX4 parameters, and load failsafe settings. In simulation it connects automatically. Parameters are named values stored in the firmware (for example the one that enables the XRCE-DDS client). Change them in QGC under Vehicle Setup -> Parameters. Some need a reboot. Never change a parameter on the real drone without knowing what it does.

Safety in the flight cage. Follow every rule below on every flight.

  • Fly in the cage with a safety pilot holding the radio transmitter. Be able to leave offboard mode with one switch and take manual control.

  • Know the kill switch: it stops the motors at once. The drone falls. Use it only when the alternative is worse. Find its channel in QGC: the parameter RC_MAP_KILL_SW shows it. Ask the safety pilot which physical switch that is.

  • Test everything in simulation first. Then fly low and slow, with props on only for a planned flight. Remove propellers when working on the bench.

  • If the setpoint stream stops, PX4 leaves offboard mode (see above). On our drone it then lands (PX4 parameter COM_OBL_RC_ACT).

6 How it fits together

The sensor produces data. Your perception node turns it into something the controller can use. Your controller node reads the vehicle state from PX4 (through the bridge), computes a command, and publishes an OffboardControlMode and a TrajectorySetpoint, as in PX4, and PX4 flies it. In simulation, Gazebo plays the part of the real world, and your nodes run the same way.
